subject: Neurology
vignette: A 45-year-old man suddenly loses all vision in his left eye while the right eye remains normal. There is no facial weakness or sensory loss. The ophthalmologist localizes the lesion to a single structure anterior to the optic chiasm.
question: Which of the following lesions best explains complete loss of vision in one eye?
explanation_correct: A lesion of the optic nerve before the chiasm interrupts all visual information from that eye, producing ipsilateral anopia, or complete blindness of the affected eye. Because the fibers have not yet crossed, only the eye on the side of the lesion is affected. This is distinct from the bilateral field deficits that arise from lesions at or beyond the chiasm.

explanation_incorrect.A: An optic chiasm lesion damages crossing nasal retinal fibers and produces bitemporal hemianopia, not monocular blindness.
explanation_incorrect.C: An optic tract lesion causes contralateral homonymous hemianopia affecting both eyes, not loss of vision in a single eye.
explanation_incorrect.D: A right visual cortex lesion produces left homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing, not anopia of one eye.
explanation_incorrect.E: A Meyer loop lesion produces a contralateral upper quadrantanopia, a partial deficit in both eyes, not monocular blindness.

educationalObjective: Optic nerve lesions cause ipsilateral anopia because they interrupt all fibers from that eye before the chiasm.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 45-year-old woman with a pituitary macroadenoma reports bumping into objects on both sides. Formal perimetry shows loss of the outer half of the visual field in each eye, with central vision preserved. The tumor is compressing the optic chiasm from below.
question: Which visual field deficit is most likely in this patient?
explanation_correct: At the optic chiasm, fibers from the nasal halves of both retinas cross, while temporal retinal fibers remain ipsilateral. A midline chiasmal lesion such as a pituitary tumor interrupts the crossing nasal fibers, which carry the temporal visual fields, producing bitemporal hemianopia. Central vision is initially preserved.

explanation_incorrect.A: Left homonymous hemianopia results from a right optic tract or right cortical lesion, not a chiasmal lesion.
explanation_incorrect.B: Anopia of one eye indicates an optic nerve lesion before the chiasm, not compression of the chiasm itself.
explanation_incorrect.C: Binasal hemianopia would require damage to the noncrossing temporal retinal fibers, which is not the pattern produced by a pituitary tumor at the chiasm.
explanation_incorrect.E: A left upper quadrantanopia would arise from a Right temporal (Meyer loop) lesion, not from chiasmal compression.

educationalObjective: Pituitary tumors compress the chiasm and cause bitemporal hemianopia by interrupting crossing nasal retinal fibers.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 28-year-old man sustains a left temporal lobe injury. Perimetry demonstrates loss of the upper-right quarter of the visual field in both eyes. The clinician attributes this to involvement of the ventral optic radiation.
question: Which visual field deficit is expected from a lesion of the left temporal (Meyer) loop?

options.text: Right homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing

explanation_correct: The ventral optic radiation, or Meyer loop, carries fibers from the lower retina and courses through the temporal lobe around the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle. A left temporal lesion therefore produces a right upper quadrantanopia. Because retinal images are upside down and left-right reversed, damage to lower retinal fibers causes a superior visual field deficit on the contralateral side.

explanation_incorrect.B: Right lower quadrantanopia results from a left parietal lesion affecting the dorsal optic radiation, which carries superior retinal fibers.
explanation_incorrect.C: A left upper quadrantanopia would follow a right temporal (Meyer loop) lesion, not a left temporal lesion.
explanation_incorrect.D: Bitemporal hemianopia arises from optic chiasm compression, not from a temporal lobe radiation lesion.
explanation_incorrect.E: Right homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing follows a right occipital cortical (PCA) infarct, not a left temporal tract lesion.

educationalObjective: A left temporal Meyer loop lesion causes right upper quadrantanopia because it interrupts lower retinal fibers.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A patient with a left parietal lobe tumor has difficulty seeing objects in the lower-right portion of the visual field of both eyes. The tumor involves the dorsal optic radiation as it travels through the parietal lobe.
question: Which tract's interruption best explains this deficit?
explanation_correct: The dorsal optic radiation carries fibers from the superior retina through the parietal lobe. A left parietal lesion affecting this tract produces a right lower quadrantanopia. Because the retinal image is inverted, superior retinal fibers correspond to the lower visual field, and the crossing at the chiasm makes the deficit contralateral.

explanation_incorrect.A: The Meyer loop is the ventral radiation through the temporal lobe and would cause an upper quadrantanopia, not a lower one.
explanation_incorrect.B: The optic chiasm is a midline structure; its lesions produce bitemporal hemianopia, not a unilateral lower quadrant deficit.
explanation_incorrect.D: An optic nerve lesion would cause monocular anopia of one eye rather than a homonymous quadrantanopia affecting both eyes.
explanation_incorrect.E: The ciliospinal tract is a sympathetic pathway involved in pupil dilation and would not produce a visual field deficit.

educationalObjective: A left parietal dorsal radiation lesion causes right lower quadrantanopia by interrupting superior retinal fibers.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 70-year-old woman has an infarct involving the left occipital visual cortex. She has a right homonymous hemianopia, but visual acuity testing shows that her central (macular) vision is preserved. The neurologist comments on 'macular sparing.'
question: Which of the following best explains this pattern of vision loss?

options.text: Middle cerebral artery occlusion with sparing of the optic radiations
Anterior cerebral artery occlusion with preserved central representation
Posterior communicating artery aneurysm compressing CN II
Optic chiasm compression from a pituitary tumor
Posterior cerebral artery infarct with macular sparing due to dual blood supply

explanation_correct: A left occipital cortical infarct in the posterior cerebral artery territory produces right homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing. The macula is spared because it has bilateral cortical representation and a dual blood supply, so central vision survives even when one occipital pole is destroyed. This cortical pattern is distinguished from tract lesions, which produce a homonymous hemianopia without macular sparing.

explanation_incorrect.A: An MCA occlusion affects lateral cortex and would not selectively produce a homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.
explanation_incorrect.B: An ACA occlusion primarily affects the medial frontal and parietal cortex and does not produce this occipital visual field pattern.
explanation_incorrect.C: A PCom aneurysm compresses CN III, causing a blown pupil and down-and-out gaze, not a cortical field deficit.
explanation_incorrect.D: Pituitary compression of the chiasm produces bitemporal hemianopia, not homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.

educationalObjective: PCA infarcts of the visual cortex cause homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing because the macula has dual blood supply and bilateral representation.
